name: Rafael Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for a side. Everything you say is confidential. What happens on a normal day at Dockside?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I catch the early bus to the office and open a pile of invoices from electricians and decorators. I'm Rafael Moreau, forty-three, and I prepare their accounts and tax returns at Dockside Accountancy. I finished a bachelor's in accounting after years in an auto-parts warehouse, so I'm a junior and still ask my supervisor about unusual expenses. I use an AI email assistant now and then after a colleague tests a feature.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like getting a trader's records straight enough that they can see whether a job actually made money. The filing deadline makes me rush, which is when I make mistakes. My partner Tessa works regular shifts at a care home, our children are eight and twelve, and we have a mortgage. My pay is about usual for this job, we have three months of expenses saved, and there are some other firms within a commute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A quiet outcome would be welcome after all the software demonstrations. I use a drafting assistant now and then for client emails, but I still find the wrong numbers by reading the invoice stack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues to keep the tool that saves a little time and measure its mistakes. I'd tell clients that the person checking their return is still part of the fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our household would probably be all right. I'm forty-three and junior at Dockside Accountancy after a late move from an auto-parts warehouse, so I am still learning tax work. Tessa's care-home shifts are regular, my pay is normal for this job, and we have three months of expenses saved with some firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on preparing tradespeople's accounts with my supervisor checking the unusual returns. I'd keep the existing hundred-and-fifty monthly transfer into savings. In the first year of a plateau, I'd use the tested email assistant on routine client reminders and request a paid hour each fortnight to review my tax-code errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the mortgage and work, even if the filing rush stays unpleasant. Tessa and I can cover an ordinary broken appliance without borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake are you still learning from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A painter's invoice was for scaffolding hire, but I first put it under equipment owned by the business. My supervisor caught it before the return went out. I keep the scaffolding invoice in my training folder because I misclassified it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the paid review hour cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show my supervisor the three tax-code mistakes I made this month and ask for a paid review hour. If the firm cannot spare the hour, I'd use the existing team guidance and keep asking questions on files. I won't take an expensive course for a small plateau.

say: I would keep **measured tools** for routine reminders.
I would tell clients **human review** remains in their fee.
think: Our **three-month cushion** can cover an ordinary repair.
My **junior skills** still need practice, even with small AI gains.
do: Keep **supervised trade accounts** and tested email reminders.
Transfer **one hundred fifty monthly** into savings.
Request a **paid review hour** for tax-code mistakes.
feel: I feel **calm** about our bills and work.
S0.quote: I keep the scaffolding invoice in my training folder because I misclassified it.
fieldNote: A **three-month cushion** and steady second wage give him security in the plateau.
The **scaffolding error** keeps him honest about junior skill despite a degree and prior warehouse experience.

steps.text: Keep supervised tradespeople returns and tested routine email drafts
Transfer one hundred fifty monthly into household savings
Review tax-code errors with supervisor if paid hour granted

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would reach my drafting and checking work first. I could learn the new review screen, but a firm might decide it needs fewer juniors before I have finished learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners for error and staffing figures together. At the union meeting I'd ask for paid training and a rule that vacancies are discussed before somebody's hours are removed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own hours could shrink, though I do not expect an immediate dismissal. I came into accounting late and am not the fastest on tax exceptions. Three months saved and a few nearby firms give us some time, but Tessa's care-home wage would not carry the mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to test the new checker on twelve tradespeople's returns after another firm has shown it works. I'd log wrong flags and take the list to the union branch. If the partners reduce my days, I'd apply for the funded warehouse accounts post if its advertised pay covers our mortgage and its start date is firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing hours, not frozen. I can test a tool and ask for a fair rule, but neither guarantees the rota stays whole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change at home if hours fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter Jo has a school trip in spring, and I would not cancel it over a rumour. If my rota loses a day, Tessa and I would cut the restaurant night before touching school money. We would use savings for the gap only while a new wage was actually in sight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you move to the warehouse post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union to put the vacancy rule in writing before the trial finishes. The warehouse post is not a plan unless it has a funded contract and an advertised salary. I would stay employed until there is a signed start date.

say: I would ask for **errors and staffing** on one page.
I would seek **paid training** and vacancy talks through the union.
think: My **hours** could shrink as routine checking moves to software.
Three months saved cannot replace a **full mortgage wage**.
do: Test **twelve returns** only after the checker works elsewhere.
Take **wrong flags** to the union for vacancy rules.
Apply for the **funded warehouse post** only if hours fall, pay covers mortgage and start is signed; otherwise stay employed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible day lost.
S1.quote: The warehouse post is not a plan unless it has a funded contract and an advertised salary.
fieldNote: A **proven-tool threshold** fits his slower technology adoption and gives the trial a concrete scope.
His **outside application** depends on funded work, advertised mortgage-covering pay and a firm start date.

steps.text: Learn proven AI checker by testing twelve tradespeople returns
Bring wrong flags to union branch for vacancy rules
Apply for funded warehouse post after hour cuts only with mortgage-covering wage and signed start
Keep current paid work until signed replacement start date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 is too quick for the practice to remake its whole client book. The return queue could be finished by a system while I still need my supervisor to check a scaffolding invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms must give notice and governments need to keep families housed while jobs change. I'd ask the union to demand the partners' dates for cutting routine tax work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior post to end in the first year after full AGI arrives in 2028. Almost all my day is thinking at a screen, so robots around 2031 do not give me more time. We have three months saved, but Tessa's care-home pay alone won't cover the mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the annual football subscription this month and hold its seventy in cash. I'd apply now for the open depot inventory-control job only if it has a funded contract and pay above our mortgage amount. In the first year after 2028, if Dockside dismisses me, I'd claim wage support promptly and ask the lender for temporary terms before missing a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because a three-month cushion is a clock when a whole kind of desk job disappears. I can make applications, but I cannot make a depot vacancy stay open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your partner take more shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tessa's care-home rota is set a month ahead. I'd ask whether extra shifts are actually confirmed before putting them in our budget. I won't tell my children everything is fine on the strength of possible overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you avoid counting money twice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The subscription ends before the next renewal, and seventy stays in the bank rather than being counted twice. The depot job needs a written start date before I resign. If it closes, I stay at Dockside while looking beyond accounting.

say: I would demand **notice and wage support** for lost work.
I would ask the union for **cut dates**.
think: My **junior screen post** may end soon after 2028.
Three months saved and one **care-home wage** cannot hold us indefinitely.
do: Cancel the **annual football subscription** and hold its one-time seventy in cash.
Apply for **funded depot work** with mortgage-covering pay and confirmed start; if closed, keep current pay while searching.
Claim **wage support** and ask lender for temporary terms after dismissal.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about a short cash runway.
S2.quote: I won't tell my children everything is fine on the strength of possible overtime.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches his accounts desk in 2028, while robots arrive later.
He budgets **confirmed care-home shifts** only and insists on a funded depot contract with a written start date.

steps.text: Cancel annual football subscription and hold one-time seventy in cash
Apply for funded depot work only with mortgage-covering pay and confirmed start date
Keep current pay while searching if depot vacancy closes
Claim wage support after 2028 dismissal and request lender terms before cash runs out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to learn another kind of accounts work while I still draw a wage. It is not long enough to assume the next screen job will be safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dockside to pay for staff to move into client dispute work and publish real vacancies. I'd ask the union to bargain for paid placement days, not an online link.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be useful helping tradespeople untangle tax notices with a person in the room. AGI could do much of the calculation in 2031, so I would need to prove clients still value the conversation. Robots in 2034 do not extend my present desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd enrol in the tax-dispute advice course if Dockside pays the four-hundred fee and gives paid study hours. I'd handle one supervised client notice if my manager releases me from returns. In the first year after AGI in 2031, if my tax post ends, I'd apply for a funded advice vacancy only if its salary covers the mortgage. If Dockside refuses the fee or paid hours, I'd keep this wage and use free legal-aid talks instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a sequence of real tests helps. I would still keep three months saved rather than spend it all on an uncertain certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why should the firm pay when you have savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fee is affordable from savings, but the firm benefits from another service and should pay for it. If Dockside refuses paid study hours or the fee, I'd use the free legal-aid talks and keep my current role. I would not call that a qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a real test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supervised notice needs a real client and a manager who checks my answer. I cannot learn to handle an upset tax client by watching a recording. I'd ask for written feedback before looking at other vacancies.

say: I would ask for **paid dispute training** and published jobs.
I would use the union to seek **placement days**.
think: A **client conversation** could outlast some calculations if clients still want personal help.
My **three-month reserve** should not fund a speculative certificate.
do: Enrol in **dispute study** if firm pays fee and hours; otherwise keep Dockside pay and use free talks.
Handle a **supervised client notice** if manager releases me.
Apply after **2031 tax job loss** for funded advice work only if salary covers mortgage.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but able to test demand.
S3.quote: I cannot learn to handle an upset tax client by watching a recording.
fieldNote: **Firm-paid study** is his condition despite moderate savings, because the course serves the practice.
A **real client notice** with feedback tests whether advice work fits before a post-2031 application.

steps.text: Enrol in dispute course if firm funds fee and paid study hours
Handle real client notice if manager grants paid supervised time
Apply for funded advice vacancy after 2031 tax job loss if salary covers mortgage
Use free legal-aid talks and keep Dockside pay if funded study refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives Jo and her brother time to grow, and gives me time to become competent at more than routine returns. I would be fifty-three when full AGI arrives in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firms gaining time should share it through shorter working weeks and funded training. I'd want a public backstop for workers whose employers refuse, but I would still ask Dockside to act first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think standard returns will be largely automated by 2036. A client-notice adviser role could be a bridge, but I do not know if clients will pay enough for it. The 2039 robots do not lengthen my screen-work deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current savings transfer and ask the local trade association next spring about a funded advice traineeship. I'd join only if it has paid supervised cases, a funded job path, a published mortgage-covering wage and confirmed start date. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if my return role ends, I'd take a funded adviser vacancy if its salary covers the mortgage; otherwise I'd claim support while I keep looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with room to prepare. I can see the children older and the mortgage smaller, but only if our pay holds through the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you expect from your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo would be twenty-two, and her brother nineteen. I hope my children have their own plans instead of becoming our emergency account. I would keep building savings while I can still earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the traineeship terms are weak?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The association would need to show me the traineeship wage, case supervisor and real vacancy path. If any of those are missing, I'd keep working at Dockside and use free public workshops. I would not move on a brochure.

say: I would seek **shared hours** and funded learning before routine returns disappear.
I would support a **public backstop** for refused training.
think: My **tax returns** remain exposed when AGI reaches desk work in 2036.
An **adviser bridge** needs paying clients or funded posts.
do: Keep saving **one hundred fifty monthly** while employed.
Join a **funded traineeship** with paid cases, job path, mortgage-covering wage and confirmed start; otherwise keep Dockside pay and free workshops.
After **2036 tax job loss**, take a funded mortgage-covering adviser vacancy or claim support if none exists.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, provided our pay holds.
S4.quote: I hope my children have their own plans instead of becoming our emergency account.
fieldNote: The **longer runway** makes gradual skill building possible without claiming advice work is safe.
The **traineeship decision** requires paid supervision, a published mortgage-covering wage and a confirmed start date.

steps.text: Transfer one hundred fifty monthly into savings while employed
Join qualifying paid traineeship; otherwise retain Dockside pay and use free public workshops
Take funded adviser vacancy after 2036 tax job loss if salary covers mortgage
Claim support after 2036 tax job loss if no funded adviser vacancy exists

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My screen work could go before our mortgage shrinks, and three months saved is short if nearby firms cut together. Notice, a wage bridge, paid training with real client cases and a funded vacancy would help. My partner's confirmed care-home shifts help, but hoped-for overtime does not belong in our budget.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the first mistake a new adviser makes. I would want a supervisor beside me when a client opens a tax demand. A course without that practice could send me into a new job with the same old gaps.

headlineQuote: My partner's confirmed care-home shifts help, but hoped-for overtime does not belong in our budget.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Rafael is a junior accountant preparing tradespeople’s returns after changing careers.
His **accounting bachelor’s** and normal pay sit beside skills he is still building.
He uses **AI occasionally** after colleagues test it, while a supervisor reviews hard cases.
A **mortgage**, two schoolchildren and three months saved make a lost wage serious.
Some **nearby firms** provide options, but he insists on funded roles and confirmed pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his screen job while nearby firms face the same shock.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **notice**, temporary wages, supervised paid training and a funded vacancy.
